Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it

vignette: The night shift at the St. Jude Community Medical Center ended in sudden, structural failure. Ananya, thirty-two, was charting in the south wing when the support columns gave way. The sound was not a crash but a deep, grinding shriek of metal shearing through concrete, followed by a vacuum of silence that swallowed her own shouts for help. She watched dust plume through the emergency lighting like thick fog, then saw the ceiling tiles shatter and the floor beneath her buckle outward. She ran, her scrubs tangling around her ankles as the building groaned and settled into a fractured stillness. Walking out into the parking lot, she stared at the collapsed east wing, the magnitude of the engineered collapse defying any logical explanation. It was so extreme that, looking at the wreckage days later, she found it hard to believe the event actually belonged to her life. It felt detached, like a scene from a news broadcast rather than a night she had survived. In the months that followed, her attempts to make sense of the disaster never coalesced into a single account. Instead, recollections arrived as disconnected pieces that did not fit together. One morning she was struck by the image of a cracked IV pole leaning against a fallen beam. Another day, the sensory detail of cold plaster dust coating her tongue surfaced without context. She would try to trace the sequence of the collapse, to understand what happened first and what followed, but she found herself pushing the memory away before she could fully recall it. Her mind would simply cut off, leaving her standing in her kitchen with no narrative to hold onto. She recognized the pattern quickly; it was not forgetfulness, but a protective halt that triggered the moment the story grew too dense. She eventually returned to nursing, taking a position at a different hospital on the north side of the city. The daily environment there became the specific setting where her encounters with the disaster's aftermath were most concrete. While transferring a patient from a stretcher, the heavy hydraulic thud of the freight elevator echoed up the stairwell, making her freeze mid-gesture. She began to avoid the service corridors entirely, taking the long route past the loading dock doors to escape the sensation of enclosed, industrial machinery. The smell of fresh drywall and the vibration of construction tools nearby always pulled her attention downward, toward the floor, toward the possibility of another sudden drop. At her current intake appointment, Ananya described how the hospital halls still feel perpetually unstable. She is most afraid of another collapse, of the floor giving way again while she is responsible for others. She hopes to find a way to hold the story of that night together, to remember it without her mind shutting down or leaving her stranded in fragments. She wants to work without constantly bracing for the sound of structural failure, and she is finally ready to sit with the pieces long enough to see what they form.
